title: I booked a $200 flight to Panama on a whim, then decided to move there. I found the community I was missing in the US.
summary:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Chrysten Crockett, a Cleveland native who moved from Atlanta to Panama City.
I went home that night, looked up Panama City, and I was like, "Oh wow, it's a big city.
I was blown away because I had never been, and I didn't know much about the country.
Crockett said she gets a lot more for her rent in Panama City than in the US.
As a solo woman traveler, when I first got here, I didn't know what the safety situation would be like.

title: Reform says it will prioritise British-born young workers for social housing
summary:
"We're saying that the first people we should be looking after are young, British workers - under 35, young British married couples, young British veterans - who have done the right thing," he said.
Rules would be changed to reserve at least half of all social homes in England for British-born workers aged under 35, with prioritisation also given to married couples, veterans, victims of domestic violence and care leavers.
Tice claimed there were currently 540,000 existing affordable social homes occupied by overseas nationals and he wanted that to change.
The Conservative Party, which also said it would revoke the right of foreign nationals to social housing, accused Reform of "trying to catch up" with its policies.
Sir James Cleverly, shadow housing secretary, added: "The Conservatives have already set out comprehensive plans to ensure British nationals are at the front of the queue for social housing.

title: Deportees who refused to exit a US flight in Liberia are sent to Equatorial Guinea
summary:
Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren't their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say.
Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled.
The group who refused to get off the plane in Liberia on Thursday include four Cuban men, a Brazilian man and a Cameroonian woman, the person and lawyer said.
Advertisement AdvertisementA Honduran deportee aboard the flight said the group refused to disembark, saying Liberia was "not their country" and that they would face danger there.
There is no medical staff at the hotel in Equatorial Guinea where the six are being held, alongside around 40 other deported migrants, she added.

title: Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 visas, official says
summary:
Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 visas, official saystoggle caption Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty ImagesThe Trump administration is preparing to cancel 200,000 immigration visas nationwide, in what could be the largest revocation effort in U.S. history, according to an administration source familiar with the policy who was not authorized to speak on the record.
"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio's leadership, we are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right.
Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud — which is grounds for visa revocation.
Sponsor MessageThe 200,000 revocations will not happen in one fell swoop, but on a rolling basis, the administration source said.
De La Espriella was backed by the Trump administration.

title: He was waiting for his son to return from the USS Lincoln. Then Border Patrol arrested him.
summary:
Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, was arrested after leaving his house to take his car to the mechanic, according to his wife, Argelia Aviles.
Aviles' son said in a Facebook post that he has been working 12-hour work shifts for more than 250 days without a break on the USS Lincoln, which is deployed in the Middle East.
Joshua Aviles wrote in his post on Saturday that he was still on the USS Lincoln "fighting for a country that has given me everything" when he got a call about his father's detention on Saturday morning.
I don't know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly treated like a criminal," Joshua Aviles wrote.
When six months passed and his son didn't come back, Aviles was distraught, she said.

title: Fentanyl investigations dropped during Trump’s immigration crackdown, DHS watchdog says
summary:
The Department of Homeland Security’s decision last year to pull additional federal agents for immigration enforcement resulted in a dramatic drop in fentanyl investigations and seizures by the department’s investigations division, according to a federal watchdog report.
The sudden change in approach toward ongoing fentanyl-related efforts stemmed from President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, which required federal agents across the government to be pulled in for immigration arrests.
That included agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations, the body charged with combatting cartels and criminal organizations.
Accordingly, HSI prioritized immigration enforcement over fentanyl-related criminal investigations,” the report found.
That also led to a reduction in fentanyl investigations and seizures.

title: Trump wants a $103,265 fee on new H-1B visas
summary:
It would charge employers $103,265 for a new H-1B visa.
H-1B visas let US employers hire foreign workers trained in specialty fields, and the technology sector leans on them heavily.
What the rule saysThe fee would apply to petitions subject to the annual cap of 85,000 visas.
Applications were already fallingEmployers registered for about 344,000 H-1B visas last year, on figures from US Citizenship and Immigration Services.
It has also proposed scrapping the grace period that lets laid-off H-1B workers stay while they look for another job.

title: Wife of active-duty Army sergeant deported amid Trump's immigration campaign
summary:
